cards.hook: Meta won its training case and lost the doctrine.
cards.body: In Kadrey v. Meta (N.D. Cal., June 2025), Judge Chhabria granted Meta summary judgment on fair use for training Llama on the plaintiff authors' books, then spent much of the opinion explaining that the plaintiffs ran the wrong play. **He endorsed market dilution as the fourth-factor theory**: not 'the model copied my book,' but 'the model floods the market with substitutes for books like mine.' The plaintiffs never built that record, so Meta won. Practitioners reading this as an industry victory are misreading a roadmap written for the next plaintiff.
cards.depth: Contrast Bartz v. Anthropic the same month: Judge Alsup called training transformative but let claims over pirated source copies proceed, and Anthropic later settled for a reported $1.5 billion. Together the rulings relocate the exposure: acquisition of the copies and output-market harm, not training itself.

cards.hook: Stop arguing about the forecast. Bet on it.
cards.body: When both sides genuinely disagree about the future, how the film performs, whether the platform renews, the standard move is to argue toward a compromise number nobody believes. The better move is a contingent contract: **let the disagreement price the deal**. Box office bonuses, backend escalators, earnouts, renewal-triggered fee bumps all work this way. Each side accepts terms that look great under its own forecast, so both sign feeling like winners, and the party with better information reveals it through what it is willing to bet on.
cards.depth: Bazerman and Gillespie's classic warning still applies: contingent terms move the fight from signing to measurement. Define the metric, the auditor, and the accounting rules in the contract, or you have just scheduled the dispute. Hollywood's net-profits history is the museum exhibit for that failure mode.

cards.hook: It's not the screen. It's the missing contingency.
cards.body: In Patricia Kuhl's well-known experiments, nine-month-old American infants exposed to live Mandarin speakers learned to discriminate Mandarin sounds; infants given the identical content by video or audio learned essentially nothing. Researchers call it the video deficit, and it holds broadly until roughly age two and a half. But the gating variable is not the glass, it is **social contingency**: later work found toddlers can learn new words over live video chat, where the adult responds to them in real time, while prerecorded video fails. Grandparent FaceTime is closer to a live tutor than to Bluey.
cards.depth: Practical read for the one-year-old: passive video is roughly inert for language, contingent interaction is the active ingredient, and background TV mostly costs by displacing parent talk. For the three-year-old the deficit fades; good content plus a co-viewing adult who talks about it beats either alone.

cards.hook: The dividend, not the buyer, exercises your short call.
cards.body: Deep in-the-money American calls rarely get exercised for the strike; they get exercised for the dividend. The holder's test is simple: if the dividend exceeds the call's remaining extrinsic value, holding the option overnight burns money versus holding the stock. So the night before ex-dividend, **any short call carrying less extrinsic value than the dividend** is a near-certain assignment, not a coin flip. Assignment risk on those strikes is a calendar event, not a probability. Check the ex-div date before you check your delta.
cards.depth: The clean screen: look at the same-strike put. If it trades for less than the dividend, rational holders exercise the call. Index options dodge this entirely because they are European-style and cash-settled, one of the quiet reasons professionals treat SPX and single-stock short-call risk as different animals.

cards.hook: Alpha has a half-life, and it starts at publication.
cards.body: McLean and Pontiff tracked 97 return anomalies from academic journals and measured what happened after the papers came out. Reported result: returns ran about a quarter lower out-of-sample and **roughly 58% lower post-publication**, as arbitrage capital crowded in. The implication for your backtests: any signal built from published research inherits a decayed forward edge that no historical window will show you. The backtest sees the pre-publication regime. You trade the post-publication one.
cards.depth: The reported decay was strongest in liquid, low-cost names where arbitrage is easy, which is exactly the universe most retail backtests use. A workable discipline: haircut the expected return of any literature-derived signal by half before sizing, then ask whether it still clears transaction costs.

cards.hook: The training-data fight is now about provenance, not permission.
cards.body: Two 2025 rulings, Bartz v. Anthropic (Alsup) and Kadrey v. Meta (Chhabria), both found that training LLMs on books can be transformative fair use. The liability survived somewhere else: Alsup carved out Anthropic's retention of pirated shadow-library copies, and Anthropic's reported $1.5 billion settlement priced that exposure. So **diligence has moved from the model to the corpus**. Papering an AI deal now means interrogating chain of custody on the training data, not re-arguing whether training itself infringes.
cards.depth: The fair-use ground is softer than it reads: Chhabria ruled on plaintiffs' failure to prove market harm and practically invited better-argued cases, while Thomson Reuters v. Ross went against fair use on non-generative training earlier in 2025. Provenance warranties are the stable ask; fair use is still moving.

cards.hook: Arrive late, leave early. Every scene.
cards.body: The working-writer version of scene economy: enter at the last possible moment and cut before the resolution fully lands. Skip the arrival, the greeting, the settling in; open where the want is already colliding with the obstacle, and end a beat early so the next scene carries the answer. The mechanism is that **inference is engagement**: what listeners reconstruct themselves lands harder than what they are handed. Andrew Stanton's phrasing: give the audience two plus two, never four. For long-form audio, these cut points are your pacing dial.
cards.depth: David Mamet's leaked memo to his TV writing staff is the blunt reference text: every scene must show someone pursuing a specific goal against resistance, and a scene that exists only to convey information is dead drama. Late-in, early-out is that rule applied at the edit points.

cards.hook: The marshmallow test measured the household, not the kid.
cards.body: Mischel's marshmallow correlations became a parenting industry. The 2018 replication by Watts, Duncan, and Quan, with a larger and more diverse sample, reported the predictive power mostly evaporating once maternal education and family background were controlled. And Celeste Kidd's earlier experiment found children wait dramatically longer, roughly 12 minutes versus 3, when the adult running the study had just proven reliable. **Waiting is a bet on the environment**: a kid who grabs the first marshmallow in an unstable setting is being rational, not weak.
cards.depth: Kidd's design was small but clean: before the marshmallow, the experimenter either delivered or reneged on promised art supplies, and wait times tracked that history. For a 3-year-old, your follow-through ledger, promises made versus kept, is doing more work than any patience drill would.

cards.hook: A covered call and a short put are the same trade.
cards.body: By put-call parity, a covered call at strike K has the identical payoff to a short cash-secured put at the same strike and expiry. Same max profit, same breakeven, same tail exposure. **The 'safe' covered call is a naked put wearing a costume.** Retail treats one as conservative income and the other as reckless, then sizes them completely differently. If you would not sell the put, you have no business writing the call. And if the call feels prudent, your real objection to the put was always the buying-power display, not the risk.
cards.depth: The equivalence holds pre-dividend and glosses over early-assignment quirks on American options, but the economic risk is the same either way. The tell is presentation: brokers show the covered call as fully collateralized stock and the put as a scary margin reduction. Same economics, different theater.

cards.hook: New York can void the AI-clone clause you signed.
cards.body: A 2024 New York law amended its right-of-publicity statute so that a contract granting rights to a performer's **digital replica is unenforceable** when the deal lacks a reasonably specific description of the intended uses and the individual was not represented by counsel or a union collective-bargaining agreement. It aims straight at the boilerplate 'in all media now known or hereafter devised' land-grab, as applied to synthetic performances. The drafting lesson runs against instinct: vague catch-all replica language does not become more enforceable by getting broader. Past a point, breadth is what gets it voided.
cards.depth: This rhymes with California's parallel move making 'digital replica' a defined, consent-gated term in talent deals. Two of the largest talent markets now police replica clauses at contract formation, not just at infringement. Overbroad synthetic-rights language has flipped from leverage into a drafting liability.

cards.hook: The flight instructors learned the wrong lesson from randomness.
cards.body: Kahneman watched Israeli Air Force instructors insist that praising a good maneuver made the next one worse, while chewing out a bad one made the next one better. They had the arrow of causation backwards. Extreme performances are partly luck, so they **regress toward the mean** no matter what the instructor says. A brilliant pass is usually followed by a duller one; a terrible pass by a better one. The feedback was pure noise, but it trained a generation of instructors that punishment beats reward. Any system that reacts to outliers will absorb the same false lesson.
cards.depth: This is why the sophomore slump, the magazine-cover jinx, and the manager fired after one bad quarter all look causal and mostly are not. Before crediting an intervention, ask what the metric would have done untouched. Reversion is the null hypothesis your intuition never bothers to run.

cards.hook: Your backtest knew the earnings before the company reported them.
cards.body: Most fundamental datasets are stored by fiscal-period date, not by the date the number actually hit the tape. So a backtest that buys 'cheap on Q1 earnings' is often trading on data the public did not have for another six to eight weeks. Worse, the figures are frequently the **restated** versions, cleaned up after amendments the live market never saw. Both errors flatter the strategy in exactly the direction you were hoping for, which is precisely why they survive review. The only real fix is point-in-time data: strictly what was knowable on the day you claim to have traded.
cards.depth: Look-ahead bias is insidious because it does not look like cheating. Nothing in your code peeks at the future; the data itself is timestamped wrong. Vendors charge a premium for 'point-in-time' feeds precisely because faithfully reconstructing what was known on a past date is hard and expensive.

cards.hook: For 20 years, networks were banned from owning their hits.
cards.body: In 1970 the FCC adopted the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules, barring the three broadcast networks from holding a financial stake in most of the prime-time entertainment they aired, or from syndicating it themselves. The point was to loosen the networks' grip and let independent producers keep the lucrative back end. It worked, for a while. **Fin-syn built the independent studio business.** Then the rules were dismantled by 1993, and within a few years ABC merged into Disney, the rest followed, and the networks owned their pipelines again. The wall stood for about one generation.
cards.depth: The rhyme is loud in streaming: platforms that once licensed everyone's shows now overwhelmingly want to own them, for the same back-end economics fin-syn was fighting over. Vertical integration is this industry's resting state. Regulation is the temporary interruption, not the other way around.

cards.hook: Sell an index straddle and you are really shorting correlation.
cards.body: When you sell an index straddle, the price you collect is set less by how much stocks move than by how much they move together. Index variance equals the weighted sum of single-stock variances plus every pairwise covariance, so implied correlation is the real lever. Dealers charge a premium for it because correlation spikes exactly when you need diversification most, in a crash. **Index vol is expensive because correlation is expensive.** The dispersion trade, short index vol and long single-name vol, isolates that premium directly.
cards.depth: The catch: implied correlation mean-reverts but jumps toward 1.0 in panics, so the position is short a convex tail. September 2008 and March 2020 both saw realized correlation gap upward, punishing naive dispersion sellers. The premium is real over full cycles, but the drawdowns cluster with everything else you own.

cards.hook: Try enough strategies and randomness will hand you a winner.
cards.body: Run twenty uncorrelated backtests on pure noise and the best one posts a Sharpe well above zero by chance alone. The problem is not any single test, it is that you only keep the survivor. Every parameter you swept, every variant you tried, every idea you quietly discarded is a hidden trial that inflates the winner you saved. **The more you search, the higher the bar a real edge must clear.** A Sharpe of 1.0 from one honest test beats a 2.0 pulled from a thousand.
cards.depth: Bailey and Lopez de Prado formalized this as the deflated Sharpe ratio, which discounts your best result by how many trials produced it and how skewed the returns are. The practical fix: log every variant you test, not just the keeper, and hold out a slice of data you never once looked at while building.

cards.hook: A likeness buyout does not survive the move to AI replicas.
cards.body: The old talent release bought a use in perpetuity for a lump sum. The SAG-AFTRA AI terms break that model. Under the 2023 and 2024 agreements, a **digital replica requires informed consent specific to each new use**, not a one-time signature covering everything downstream. A performer who consented to a replica for one film has not consented to a sequel, an ad, or a training set. The negotiating fight has quietly shifted from price-per-role to who controls the replica after the cameras stop.
cards.depth: The practitioner error is drafting AI-era likeness rights as a traditional buyout. California's AB 2602 voids digital-replica contract terms unless the intended use is described with reasonable specificity, and AB 1836 adds post-mortem consent. Scope the grant use by use, or expect to renegotiate later at leverage you no longer hold.

cards.hook: More data made the experts confident, not correct.
cards.body: In a classic study, professional handicappers predicted horse races given five, then ten, twenty, and forty variables. As the data grew, their **confidence climbed steadily while their accuracy stayed flat.** By forty variables they were far more sure and no more right. The extra information mostly fed the story they already believed. For a trader building a thesis or a lawyer building a position, this is the trap: each confirming detail feels like progress but often just inflates certainty. The useful question is not what else supports the view, but what would break it.
cards.depth: The mechanism is that new data rarely arrives neutral, we recruit it to defend a prior. Calibration research finds the cure is not more inputs but forced disconfirmation: name the two facts that would most change your mind before you gather more. Traders call it the exit thesis. Lawyers call it the other side's best argument.

cards.hook: Trade issues you value differently instead of splitting each one.
cards.body: Most negotiations grind issue by issue, splitting the difference on each. That is how value gets destroyed. When two sides weight the same issues differently, the gains come from **trading concessions across issues, not compromising within them.** Give ground where you care little to win where you care a lot, and invite the counterparty to do the same. Research on integrative bargaining calls this logrolling, and negotiators who probe for it consistently reach larger and more durable deals than those who haggle line by line.
cards.depth: The prerequisite is information: you cannot trade across priorities you have not surfaced. Skilled negotiators ask more diagnostic questions and float multiple-issue offers rather than single-issue ultimatums, which reveals relative weights without conceding position. The failure mode is the fixed-pie assumption, the reflex belief that the other side wants exactly what you want. Usually they do not.

cards.hook: The variance premium hides in the strikes you fear most.
cards.body: Implied volatility sits above subsequent realized volatility most of the time, and that gap is your pay for underwriting other people's fear. But it is not spread evenly. The persistent bid for downside protection means **out-of-the-money puts carry the richest premium relative to what actually gets realized**. The strikes that feel most dangerous to sell are, on average, the best compensated. Selling the whole surface uniformly leaves the fattest part of the edge on the table.
cards.depth: The catch is path. Those same strikes deliver the deepest drawdowns when a crash finally arrives, so the premium is real but so is the tail. Size for the gap risk, not the average, and the edge survives the regime that pays for it.

cards.hook: Denmark wants to copyright your own face.
cards.body: In 2025 Denmark's culture ministry announced a proposal to amend its copyright law so every citizen would hold rights over their own body, facial features, and voice. The target is deepfakes: a property-style claim people could use to force removal of synthetic likenesses they never consented to. This is a reported proposal, not yet enacted, but the framing matters. **Most jurisdictions treat likeness as a publicity or privacy right; Denmark is reaching for copyright's takedown machinery instead.**
cards.depth: Copyright brings notice-and-takedown, statutory remedies, and cross-border treaties that publicity rights lack. If it passes, platforms would face likeness claims through the same DMCA-style pipes they already run for music and film, which is a very different enforcement cost curve than tort-based right-of-publicity litigation.

cards.hook: Your 90% confident range is wrong about half the time.
cards.body: Ask people for a range they are 90 percent sure contains some unknown value, and across decades of studies the true value falls outside that range far more than 10 percent of the time, often closer to 40 or 50 percent. The label says 90; the calibration says coin flip. **We build intervals too narrow because we anchor on our best guess and add token padding instead of imagining how we could be wrong.** The fix is deliberate: state the interval, then widen it until it genuinely feels too wide.
cards.depth: This is overconfidence in its most measurable form, documented by Alpert and Raiffa and later by Russo and Schoemaker. Traders feel it as stops that keep getting hit: the price lived in the tail you had priced out. Tracking your own hit rate closes the gap surprisingly fast.

cards.hook: Your backtest filled at a price the market never offered.
cards.body: Most backtests assume you transacted at the closing print or the midpoint of the bid-ask spread. You did not. Real fills cross the spread, move the market, and miss entirely when liquidity vanishes exactly as your signal fires. **A strategy's edge and its trading costs are usually correlated, because the same volatility that triggers your entries also widens the spreads you pay to get in.** Strip out realistic costs and many high-turnover backtests that looked brilliant collapse to break-even or worse.
cards.depth: Model costs as a function of spread, size, and volatility at the moment of the trade, not a flat per-share fee. Then stress it: double the assumed slippage. If the edge dies, it was never edge. It was an accounting artifact of fills you could not have gotten.

cards.hook: One actress capped every Hollywood contract at seven years.
cards.body: In the studio era a seven-year contract was not really seven years. When a star refused a role, the studio suspended her and tacked the lost time onto the end, so contracts stretched almost indefinitely. Olivia de Havilland sued Warner Bros., and in 1944 California's courts ruled that the seven-year limit in Labor Code section 2855 runs on the calendar, not on time actually worked. **Suspensions could no longer extend the term.** The ruling broke the studios' core mechanism of control over talent.
cards.depth: The rule still carries her name, the De Havilland Law, and section 2855 still caps personal-service contracts at seven calendar years. It resurfaces whenever long recording or streaming deals get challenged, most visibly in fights over multi-album music contracts decades after the original decision.

cards.hook: You are not paid theta. You are paid for gamma.
cards.body: Theta decay feels like income, but it is compensation, not yield. Every dollar of decay you collect is payment for the **gamma you are short**: the obligation to lose money at an accelerating rate when the underlying moves. Short-dated options look juicy precisely because their gamma is exploding. When a premium seller says 'I earn theta,' the market hears 'I sell crash insurance.' Both are true. The edge question is never 'how much theta' but 'is the insurance overpriced right now.'
cards.depth: This is why identical-delta positions at 45 DTE vs 7 DTE behave so differently: the 7 DTE position collects more theta per day but its P&L distribution is far more violent per point of underlying movement. Same premium, different insurance book.

cards.hook: Your best backtest is mostly selection bias
cards.body: Test 100 strategy variants and pick the winner: its backtested Sharpe is inflated almost by construction, because you selected for luck along with skill. This is the **multiple-testing problem**, and it is the single biggest reason live results disappoint. Finance researchers (Bailey and Lopez de Prado) formalized it as the 'deflated Sharpe ratio': the more configurations you tried, the higher the bar your winner must clear before you believe it. Most retail backtesting never counts the trials.
cards.depth: Practical discipline: log every variant you test, not just winners. Decide the strategy logic BEFORE optimizing parameters. And hold out a chunk of data you only touch once, at the very end. If you peeked at it twice, it is not a holdout anymore.

cards.hook: Tennessee got to AI voice rights before Congress did
cards.body: The ELVIS Act (Tennessee, effective July 2024) was the first state statute to explicitly add **voice** to right-of-publicity protection with AI simulation in mind, and it reaches tools 'primarily designed' to produce unauthorized voice clones, not just outputs. Meanwhile the federal NO FAKES Act remains proposed, not law. The practical map: state patchwork now governs synthetic likeness, and choice-of-law plus where the plaintiff lives quietly became the first question in every deepfake dispute.
cards.depth: For deal work: the interesting drafting problem is that most legacy talent agreements granted 'voice' rights before voice cloning existed. Whether an old grant covers a new synthetic use is the fight; the ELVIS Act tilts leverage toward talent in Tennessee-connected disputes.

cards.hook: Amateurs ask what happened. Pros ask what usually happens.
cards.body: Reference-class forecasting: before estimating your specific case, find the base rate for the **class of cases it belongs to**. Kahneman calls ignoring this the 'inside view' trap: your case always feels exceptional because you know its details. Planning a product launch? The relevant question is not 'how good is our plan' but 'what fraction of launches like this hit their date.' The outside view is usually humbling, and it is usually right. Start there, then adjust for specifics, sparingly.
cards.depth: Tetlock's forecasting tournaments found the same move in top performers: they anchor on base rates first, then update in small increments. The failure mode of smart people is not ignorance; it is treating their own case as exempt from the statistics.

cards.hook: Hollywood spent 70 years rebuilding the thing the government broke
cards.body: In 1948 the Supreme Court's Paramount decision forced the studios to sell their theater chains: production divorced from distribution and exhibition. That consent-decree regime lasted until the DOJ terminated it in **2020**, right as streaming completed the loop the decrees had cut. Netflix, Amazon, and Apple now produce, distribute, and 'exhibit' in one pipe, vertical integration the 1948 court would have recognized instantly. The industry's structure did not evolve; it circled.
cards.depth: The rhyme worth watching: the decrees fell partly because 'the market changed.' Every consolidation cycle in media has been justified the same way, and every one has eventually produced the same complaint: the pipe owner favors its own product.

cards.hook: The premium seller's real product is regret insurance
cards.body: Index implied volatility has historically averaged a few points above subsequently realized volatility. That gap, the **variance risk premium**, is the structural reason systematic premium selling has positive expectancy over long windows. But it is not free money: the premium exists because buyers rationally overpay to avoid catastrophic left-tail outcomes, and sellers periodically eat exactly those outcomes. You are running a small insurance company. Insurance companies are profitable on average and occasionally destroyed by a single storm they mispriced.
cards.depth: The regime question matters more than the strategy question: the VRP compresses or inverts around stress. Sizing so that the storm year is survivable is the whole game; the average year takes care of itself.

cards.hook: The task you left keeps billing you for 20 minutes
cards.body: Sophie Leroy's research on **attention residue**: when you switch tasks, part of your cognitive capacity stays attached to the unfinished task, degrading performance on the new one, often for 20+ minutes. The residue is worst when the abandoned task was unfinished and time-pressured. This is why a 'quick check' of email before deep work is so expensive: you pay the interruption twice, once in time and again in residue. Closing a task with a written next-step note measurably reduces the carryover.
cards.depth: Practical version: before switching, write one line about exactly where you stopped and what happens next. The note gives your brain permission to release the open loop. Cheap ritual, real effect.

cards.hook: Two Nobel Prizes, 25x leverage, one dead fund
cards.body: Long-Term Capital Management employed Merton and Scholes, produced ~40% annual returns, and in 1998 lost roughly **$4.6 billion in a few months** when Russia defaulted and every 'uncorrelated' convergence trade converged to panic simultaneously. The lesson is not 'smart people fail.' It is that correlations you measured in calm markets are a fiction in stressed ones, because in a crisis everyone holds the same trades and everyone must sell at once. Leverage turns that fiction fatal.
cards.depth: The Fed brokered a private bailout because LTCM's positions were so large that liquidation threatened the system. Every vol seller should read the LTCM story annually as a memento mori: their models were right on average. Average was not the problem.

cards.hook: The rally matters more than the vocabulary
cards.body: Harvard's Center on the Developing Child calls it **serve and return**: a child initiates (babble, point, glance), an adult responds contingently, the child responds back. These rallies, not passive word exposure, are the strongest documented driver of early language and executive-function wiring. A toddler's endless 'why' phase is a serve. The developmental payload is in the return being contingent and prompt, not in it being correct or educational. Flashcards lose to volleys.
cards.depth: This reframes screen time too: the documented issue is less the screen than the missing contingency. A video cannot return a serve. Same reason video-chat with a grandparent behaves differently in studies than passive viewing: the rally survives the screen.

cards.hook: Your data is haunted by companies that no longer exist
cards.body: Backtest a stock strategy on today's ticker universe and you have quietly excluded every company that went bankrupt or delisted along the way: **survivorship bias**. The dead ones were disproportionately the value traps and momentum crashes your strategy would have bought. Studies of the effect find it can inflate apparent returns materially, enough to turn a losing strategy into a 'winner.' Free data sources are the worst offenders because dead tickers are expensive to maintain.
cards.depth: The same ghost haunts fund performance tables (dead funds vanish from averages) and option strategies tested only through periods where the underlying survived. First question for any backtest: who is missing from this dataset, and did they die of exactly what I'm about to buy?

cards.hook: Replace every 'and then' with 'but' or 'therefore'
cards.body: The South Park writers' room rule: if you can describe your story as 'this happens, AND THEN this happens,' it is dead on the page. Every beat should connect to the next by **'but' or 'therefore'**: a goal meets an obstacle, a consequence forces a choice. 'And then' is a list; 'but/therefore' is causality, and causality is what audiences experience as momentum. It is the fastest story diagnostic that exists: read your outline aloud and listen for which connector you're using.
cards.depth: Works on legal storytelling too. A demand letter or a jury narrative built on 'therefore' chains reads as inevitable; one built on 'and then' reads as a timeline. Inevitability is persuasion.

cards.hook: Precise numbers anchor harder than round ones
cards.body: Negotiation research (Janiszewski and Uy) found that **precise first offers produce smaller counter-adjustments** than round ones: $4,850 outperforms $5,000 as an anchor. The mechanism: a precise number implies underlying calculation, so counterparties adjust in finer increments, while a round number reads as a placeholder inviting a big swing. Combined with the robust finding that first offers strongly predict final outcomes, the playbook writes itself: anchor first when you have information, and anchor in odd increments.
cards.depth: The caveat practitioners miss: extreme-but-precise anchors can backfire by signaling bad faith and killing deals that had positive surplus. Precision buys you credibility only inside the plausible range. Outside it, precision reads as manipulation.

cards.hook: Full Kelly is a rollercoaster you never need to ride
cards.body: The Kelly criterion gives the bet size that maximizes long-run growth, and almost no professional bets it. Full Kelly's price is brutal variance: drawdowns deep enough to break the discipline that the formula assumes you have. **Half-Kelly captures roughly three-quarters of the growth rate at a fraction of the drawdown pain**, which is why it is the practitioner default. The deeper lesson: your true edge estimate is uncertain, and betting full Kelly on an overestimated edge is how accounts die.
cards.depth: Kelly assumes you know your edge and odds exactly. You never do. Sizing at half-Kelly is equivalent to admitting your edge estimate might be roughly half wrong, which, empirically, is generous. When in doubt, the error that kills you is oversizing, never undersizing.

cards.hook: Clever scaffolding loses to compute. Eventually. Always.
cards.body: Rich Sutton's 'Bitter Lesson,' distilled from 70 years of AI research: methods that leverage **general computation and learning** eventually beat methods built on hand-encoded human knowledge, every time, in every domain. Chess heuristics lost to search; linguistic features lost to transformers. The builder's implication: elaborate prompt scaffolding and rule chains are depreciating assets. Build the thin harness that lets a smarter model do more, not the thick one that compensates for today's model, because today's model is temporary.
cards.depth: The practical test for any AI workflow you build: 'does this get MORE valuable when the model improves, or less?' Pipelines that route, verify, and give models context appreciate. Pipelines that micromanage reasoning depreciate. Sort your projects into those two buckets honestly.

cards.hook: The trade that made 'short vol' a horror genre
cards.body: February 5, 2018, 'Volmageddon': the VIX spiked over 100% in a day and XIV, an exchange-traded note that profited from falling volatility, lost roughly **96% of its value overnight** and was terminated by its issuer. The mechanics were the killer: XIV's own end-of-day rebalancing forced massive VIX-futures buying into a spiking market, accelerating the spike that was killing it. A product whose hedging flow amplifies the exact move that destroys it is not an investment; it is a fuse.
cards.depth: The generalizable screen: for any yield-like product, ask 'what does its own rebalancing do in the tail?' If the answer is 'buys what is exploding or sells what is collapsing,' the historical Sharpe is an illusion priced before the fuse lit.

cards.hook: Testing yourself beats re-reading. It isn't close.
cards.body: Roediger and Karpicke's retrieval-practice studies: students who **tested themselves** on material retained dramatically more a week later than students who re-read it, even though re-readers felt more confident. The act of pulling a memory out strengthens it far more than pushing it in again. Fluency from re-reading is a feeling, not a fact. This is also why this feed occasionally asks you what an old card said instead of telling you: the ask is the mechanism.
cards.depth: Corollary for professionals: the highest-yield review of any domain is closed-book. Summarize the deal structure, the doctrine, the strategy from memory first, THEN check the source. The gap you find is the actual study list.

cards.hook: California made 'digital replica' a defined term in every talent deal
cards.body: AB 2602 (effective January 2025) makes a contract provision unenforceable if it allows creating or using a **digital replica** of a performer's voice or likeness in place of work the performer would otherwise have done, unless the use is specifically described and the performer had counsel or union representation in the deal. Translation for practitioners: boilerplate 'in perpetuity, in any media now known or hereafter devised' no longer quietly captures synthetic re-performance in California. The replica clause is now its own negotiation.
cards.depth: Paired statute AB 1836 extended postmortem publicity rights to digital replicas of deceased performers. Together they mark the pattern: California regulating synthetic performance through contract-formation rules and estates law rather than waiting for federal preemption that may never come.

cards.hook: Forrest Gump grossed $678 million and 'lost money'
cards.body: Winston Groom, whose novel became Forrest Gump, took **3% of net profits**. The film grossed roughly $678 million worldwide; by studio accounting it was reportedly still in deficit years later, so his net points initially paid essentially nothing. Distribution fees, overhead charges, and interest, all paid to the studio's own divisions, consumed the 'profit' before it reached net. The industry knew; that is why gross points versus net points was already the dividing line between leverage and hope.
cards.depth: The evergreen practitioner lesson: a percentage is only as valuable as the defined pool it draws from. In any waterfall, the definitions section IS the deal. That principle transfers intact to streaming bonuses, creator rev-shares, and AI-content royalty pools being drafted right now.

cards.hook: A strategy that worked for 15 years can be one regime old
cards.body: Long backtests feel rigorous, but markets are not a stationary process: they are a sequence of **regimes** (rate environments, vol structures, market microstructure) stitched together. A 15-year test spanning one long low-rate regime is closer to a single observation than to 15. Walk-forward testing, splitting history into rolling train/validate windows, at least forces the strategy to survive regime seams. The honest question is never 'did it work historically' but 'which regime was doing the work, and is that regime still here?'
cards.depth: Cheap diagnostic: plot your strategy's rolling 12-month performance against a regime marker (VIX level, rate direction, term-structure state). If all the P&L clusters in one regime state, you have not found an edge; you have found a regime bet wearing a strategy costume.

cards.hook: Starting is a different brain function than doing
cards.body: Task initiation and task execution are separable executive functions, which is why you can be excellent at hard work you cannot start. The research-backed exploits all shrink the initiation step rather than motivating the execution: **implementation intentions** ('when X happens, I do Y') roughly double follow-through rates in Gollwitzer's meta-analyses, and 'do it for five minutes' works because initiation, not effort, was the bottleneck. Willpower framing treats a wiring difference as a character flaw, then wonders why shame doesn't ship work.
cards.depth: The strongest version pairs a trigger with a location and time: 'after daycare drop-off, in the car, I send one outreach message.' Specificity is the active ingredient; vague intentions ('do more outreach') showed almost no effect in the same studies.
